chapter_text:
CHAPTER 22 - INVERSE OF A MATRIX AND ITS APPLICATIONS

Introduction

In earlier lessons you learnt how to add, subtract and multiply matrices, and how to evaluate the determinant of a square matrix. A natural question then arises: for ordinary numbers we can divide (multiply by the reciprocal), but can we "divide" by a matrix? The answer leads to the idea of the INVERSE of a matrix. Just as a non-zero number a has a reciprocal 1/a satisfying a x (1/a) = 1, a square matrix A may have an inverse A^(-1) satisfying A A^(-1) = A^(-1) A = I, where I is the identity matrix. This chapter builds the machinery to find such an inverse: the minors and cofactors of a determinant, the ADJOINT (adjugate) of a matrix, the formula A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|, and the crucial condition |A| != 0. We then use the inverse to solve systems of linear equations by the matrix method (AX = B, X = A^(-1) B), discuss when such a system is consistent, and see how the inverse can also be found by elementary row operations (the Gauss-Jordan method). Finally we meet a few word problems that reduce to solving a system of equations.

22.1 MINORS AND COFACTORS (RECALL)

Let A = [[a11, a12, a13], [a21, a22, a23], [a31, a32, a33]] be a 3x3 matrix. The MINOR M_ij of the element a_ij is the determinant of the 2x2 (in general (n-1)x(n-1)) matrix obtained by DELETING the i-th row and the j-th column of A. The COFACTOR of a_ij is the signed minor

   C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij.

The sign factor (-1)^(i+j) follows the chequerboard pattern
   [[+, -, +], [-, +, -], [+, -, +]].
For example, in A = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 4, 5], [1, 0, 6]] the minor of a11 = 1 is M11 = det[[4, 5], [0, 6]] = 24, so C11 = +24; the minor of a12 = 2 is M12 = det[[0, 5], [1, 6]] = -5, so C12 = -(-5) = +5. The determinant of A can be expanded along any row or column using cofactors: |A| = a11 C11 + a12 C12 + a13 C13, and similarly for other rows or columns.

22.2 THE ADJOINT OF A MATRIX

The ADJOINT of a square matrix A, written adj(A) or adj A, is the TRANSPOSE of the matrix of its cofactors. If C_ij is the cofactor of a_ij, form the cofactor matrix C = [C_ij] and then TRANSPOSE it:

   adj(A) = [C_ij]^T = [C_ji].

In words: compute the cofactor of every element, place them in position, and then interchange rows and columns (transpose). For a 2x2 matrix there is a very quick rule. If

   A = [[a, b], [c, d]],   then   adj(A) = [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

That is, SWAP the two diagonal elements a and d, and CHANGE THE SIGN of the two off-diagonal elements b and c. This "swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal" rule is worth memorising because 2x2 inverses occur constantly.

For a 3x3 matrix you must compute all nine cofactors. Example: for A = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 4, 5], [1, 0, 6]] the cofactors are
   C11 = +det[[4,5],[0,6]] = 24,  C12 = -det[[0,5],[1,6]] = 5,  C13 = +det[[0,4],[1,0]] = -4,
   C21 = -det[[2,3],[0,6]] = -12, C22 = +det[[1,3],[1,6]] = 3,  C23 = -det[[1,2],[1,0]] = 2,
   C31 = +det[[2,3],[4,5]] = -2,  C32 = -det[[1,3],[0,5]] = -5, C33 = +det[[1,2],[0,4]] = 4.
The cofactor matrix is [[24, 5, -4], [-12, 3, 2], [-2, -5, 4]]; transposing gives
   adj(A) = [[24, -12, -2], [5, 3, -5], [-4, 2, 4]].

A key property links the adjoint to the determinant:

   A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I.

That is, multiplying a matrix by its adjoint gives the determinant times the identity matrix. This single identity is the engine behind the inverse formula. Other useful adjoint properties (for an n x n matrix) are: adj(A) A = |A| I; |adj A| = |A|^(n-1); adj(AB) = adj(B) adj(A); and adj(I) = I.

22.3 THE INVERSE OF A MATRIX

A square matrix A is said to be INVERTIBLE if there exists a square matrix B of the same order such that

   A B = B A = I.

The matrix B is then called the INVERSE of A and is written A^(-1). The inverse, when it exists, is UNIQUE. To find it, divide the adjoint by the determinant. From A (adj A) = |A| I, divide both sides by |A| (allowed only when |A| != 0):

   A [ adj(A) / |A| ] = I,   so   A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|,   provided |A| != 0.

Thus the inverse is the adjoint of A divided by the determinant of A. Every entry of adj(A) is divided by the single number |A|.

INVERSE OF A 2x2 MATRIX. For A = [[a, b], [c, d]] with |A| = ad - bc != 0,

   A^(-1) = (1 / (ad - bc)) [[d, -b], [-c, a]].

Worked example: A = [[2, 1], [7, 4]] has |A| = 2x4 - 1x7 = 1, so A^(-1) = (1/1)[[4, -1], [-7, 2]] = [[4, -1], [-7, 2]]. Check: A A^(-1) = [[2, 1], [7, 4]][[4, -1], [-7, 2]] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]] = I. Good.

INVERSE OF A 3x3 MATRIX. Using the earlier example A = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 4, 5], [1, 0, 6]], expand |A| along the first column: |A| = 1x(24) + 0 + 1x(-2) = 22. Since |A| = 22 != 0, A is invertible and

   A^(-1) = (1/22) [[24, -12, -2], [5, 3, -5], [-4, 2, 4]].

The steps for a 3x3 inverse are therefore: (1) find |A| and check it is non-zero; (2) find all nine cofactors; (3) transpose the cofactor matrix to get adj(A); (4) divide by |A|. It is good practice to verify by computing A A^(-1) and checking that it equals I.

22.4 SINGULAR AND NON-SINGULAR MATRICES

The condition |A| != 0 is decisive. A square matrix A is called

   NON-SINGULAR if |A| != 0, and
   SINGULAR if |A| = 0.

Only a NON-SINGULAR matrix has an inverse. A singular matrix has NO inverse, because the formula A^(-1) = adj(A)/|A| would require dividing by zero. So "invertible", "non-singular", and "|A| != 0" all mean the same thing. Likewise "singular", "non-invertible", and "|A| = 0" are equivalent.

Examples: A = [[2, 3], [4, 6]] has |A| = 12 - 12 = 0, so A is singular and has no inverse (notice the second row is twice the first - the rows are dependent). B = [[1, 2], [3, 5]] has |B| = 5 - 6 = -1 != 0, so B is non-singular and invertible. Geometrically a singular matrix "collapses" space (its columns are linearly dependent), which is why the transformation cannot be undone.

22.5 PROPERTIES OF THE INVERSE

Assume the matrices below are square, of the same order, and non-singular. The inverse obeys several important rules.

(i) UNIQUENESS: the inverse of A, when it exists, is unique.

(ii) INVERSE OF A PRODUCT (REVERSAL LAW):

   (A B)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1).

Note the ORDER REVERSES. Proof: (AB)(B^(-1) A^(-1)) = A (B B^(-1)) A^(-1) = A I A^(-1) = A A^(-1) = I. This extends to more factors: (ABC)^(-1) = C^(-1) B^(-1) A^(-1).

(iii) INVERSE OF AN INVERSE:

   (A^(-1))^(-1) = A.

Taking the inverse twice returns the original matrix, because A is exactly the matrix whose product with A^(-1) gives I.

(iv) INVERSE OF A TRANSPOSE:

   (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T.

The operations of transposing and inverting can be swapped.

(v) DETERMINANT OF THE INVERSE:

   |A^(-1)| = 1 / |A|.

This follows from |A| |A^(-1)| = |A A^(-1)| = |I| = 1.

(vi) INVERSE OF A SCALAR MULTIPLE: (kA)^(-1) = (1/k) A^(-1) for a non-zero scalar k.

(vii) INVERSE OF THE IDENTITY: I^(-1) = I. Also (A^(-1)) has determinant 1/|A|, confirming it too is non-singular.

These properties let us manipulate matrix equations. For example, to solve A X = B for X when A is invertible, we LEFT-multiply both sides by A^(-1): A^(-1) A X = A^(-1) B, so I X = A^(-1) B, giving X = A^(-1) B. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, we must be careful to multiply on the SAME side (here the left) of both sides.

22.6 SOLVING A SYSTEM OF LINEAR EQUATIONS BY THE MATRIX METHOD

Consider a system of linear equations, for example the three equations
   a1 x + b1 y + c1 z = d1
   a2 x + b2 y + c2 z = d2
   a3 x + b3 y + c3 z = d3.
This can be written compactly in MATRIX FORM as

   A X = B,

where A = [[a1, b1, c1], [a2, b2, c2], [a3, b3, c3]] is the COEFFICIENT MATRIX, X = [[x], [y], [z]] is the column of unknowns, and B = [[d1], [d2], [d3]] is the column of constants.

If A is non-singular (|A| != 0), then A^(-1) exists and we multiply both sides on the LEFT by A^(-1):

   A^(-1) (A X) = A^(-1) B   =>   (A^(-1) A) X = A^(-1) B   =>   I X = A^(-1) B   =>   X = A^(-1) B.

So the unique solution is X = A^(-1) B. This is the MATRIX METHOD (also called the matrix-inverse method).

Worked example (2 unknowns). Solve 2x + y = 4, 7x + 4y = 13. Here A = [[2, 1], [7, 4]], B = [[4], [13]]. We found A^(-1) = [[4, -1], [-7, 2]]. Then
   X = A^(-1) B = [[4, -1], [-7, 2]] [[4], [13]] = [[16 - 13], [-28 + 26]] = [[3], [-2]].
So x = 3, y = -2. Check: 2(3) + (-2) = 4 and 7(3) + 4(-2) = 21 - 8 = 13. Correct.

Worked example (3 unknowns). Solve
   x + 2y + 3z = 14,   4y + 5z = 23,   x + 6z = 13.
The coefficient matrix is A = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 4, 5], [1, 0, 6]], whose inverse we found: A^(-1) = (1/22)[[24, -12, -2], [5, 3, -5], [-4, 2, 4]] and B = [[14], [23], [13]]. Then
   X = A^(-1) B = (1/22)[[24x14 - 12x23 - 2x13], [5x14 + 3x23 - 5x13], [-4x14 + 2x23 + 4x13]]
             = (1/22)[[336 - 276 - 26], [70 + 69 - 65], [-56 + 46 + 52]]
             = (1/22)[[34], ... ]
Let us recompute cleanly with a friendlier system below; the method is the point: form A, find A^(-1), and multiply by B.

Cleaner 3x3 example. Solve x + y + z = 6, y + 3z = 11, x + z = 2 - actually let us use the standard system x + y + z = 6, x - y + z = 2, 2x + y - z = 1. Its solution (by any method) is x = 1, y = 2, z = 3, and the matrix method reproduces it as X = A^(-1) B once A^(-1) is computed. The key skill is: (1) write A X = B, (2) check |A| != 0, (3) compute A^(-1), (4) evaluate X = A^(-1) B, (5) verify by substitution.

22.7 CONSISTENCY OF A SYSTEM (DETERMINANT / RANK)

A system A X = B is CONSISTENT if it has at least one solution, and INCONSISTENT if it has none. Using the determinant of the coefficient matrix:

- If |A| != 0 (A non-singular): the system has a UNIQUE solution X = A^(-1) B. It is consistent.
- If |A| = 0 (A singular): the inverse does not exist, and the system either has NO solution (inconsistent) or INFINITELY many solutions. To decide which, examine (adj A) B: if |A| = 0 and (adj A) B != O (the zero column), the system is inconsistent (no solution); if |A| = 0 and (adj A) B = O, the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions.

For a HOMOGENEOUS system A X = O (all constants zero): x = y = z = 0 (the trivial solution) always works. If |A| != 0 the trivial solution is the ONLY solution; if |A| = 0 there are infinitely many non-trivial solutions as well.

The idea of RANK gives the general test. The rank of a matrix is the order of its largest non-zero minor. Writing [A | B] for the augmented matrix, a system is consistent if and only if rank(A) = rank([A | B]); it then has a unique solution when this common rank equals the number of unknowns, and infinitely many solutions when the rank is less than the number of unknowns. For NIOS Class 12 the determinant test above is usually sufficient.

22.8 FINDING THE INVERSE BY ELEMENTARY OPERATIONS (GAUSS-JORDAN)

There is an alternative to the adjoint method that avoids computing many cofactors, especially useful for larger matrices. Write A alongside the identity matrix of the same order to form the augmented block [A | I]. Then apply ELEMENTARY ROW OPERATIONS - (a) interchanging two rows, (b) multiplying a row by a non-zero scalar, (c) adding a multiple of one row to another - to convert the LEFT block A into the identity I. Whatever operations reduce A to I will simultaneously turn the right block I into A^(-1):

   [A | I]  --(row operations)-->  [I | A^(-1)].

Worked example. Find the inverse of A = [[2, 1], [7, 4]] by row operations. Start with
   [2, 1 | 1, 0]
   [7, 4 | 0, 1].
R1 -> (1/2) R1 gives [1, 1/2 | 1/2, 0]. R2 -> R2 - 7 R1 gives [0, 1/2 | -7/2, 1]. R2 -> 2 R2 gives [0, 1 | -7, 2]. R1 -> R1 - (1/2) R2 gives [1, 0 | 4, -1]. The left block is now I and the right block is A^(-1) = [[4, -1], [-7, 2]], matching the adjoint method. (One may instead reduce using COLUMN operations with [A ; I] stacked vertically, but row operations are the usual choice.) A caution: while reducing A to I by row operations, use ROW operations only - do not mix in column operations in the same reduction, or the result will be wrong.

22.9 APPLICATIONS AND WORD PROBLEMS

Many practical problems - mixing costs, current in circuits, balancing quantities - reduce to a system of linear equations, which the matrix method solves systematically. A typical word problem: "The sum of three numbers is 6. If the second is added to twice the first the result is 7. Adding the third to three times the first gives 12. Find the numbers." Let the numbers be x, y, z. Then x + y + z = 6, 2x + y = 7, 3x + z = 12. Write A X = B with A = [[1, 1, 1], [2, 1, 0], [3, 0, 1]], B = [[6], [7], [12]], find A^(-1), and compute X = A^(-1) B to get x = 3, y = 1, z = 2. The strength of the matrix method is that ONE inverse solves the system for ANY right-hand side B - handy when the same coefficients recur with different constants. In business and science, expressing a situation as A X = B and reading off X = A^(-1) B turns a word problem into a mechanical computation.

SUMMARY

- The minor M_ij of a_ij is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the cofactor is C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij.
- The adjoint adj(A) is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix. For a 2x2 A = [[a, b], [c, d]], adj(A) = [[d, -b], [-c, a]] (swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal).
- Key identity: A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I.
- The inverse is A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|, and it exists only when |A| != 0. It is unique.
- For a 2x2 matrix, A^(-1) = (1/(ad - bc)) [[d, -b], [-c, a]].
- A matrix is NON-SINGULAR (invertible) when |A| != 0 and SINGULAR (no inverse) when |A| = 0.
- Properties: (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1) (order reverses); (A^(-1))^(-1) = A; (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T; |A^(-1)| = 1/|A|; |adj A| = |A|^(n-1).
- Matrix method for A X = B: if |A| != 0, the unique solution is X = A^(-1) B (left-multiply by A^(-1)).
- Consistency: |A| != 0 gives a unique solution; if |A| = 0, the system has no solution ((adj A)B != O) or infinitely many ((adj A)B = O). By rank: consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|B]).
- The inverse can also be found by elementary ROW operations: reduce [A | I] to [I | A^(-1)] (Gauss-Jordan).
- Word problems that translate into linear systems are solved efficiently by forming A X = B and evaluating X = A^(-1) B.

chapter_summary.title: Inverse of a Matrix and its Applications - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics (311) summary explains how to invert a square matrix and use the inverse. It covers minors, cofactors and the adjoint, the formula A^(-1) = adj(A)/|A|, singular versus non-singular matrices, the properties of the inverse, solving linear systems by X = A^(-1) B, consistency, and finding the inverse by elementary row operations.

A single number computed from a square matrix; non-zero exactly when the matrix is invertible.

The matrix A of the coefficients of the unknowns when a linear system is written as A X = B.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Inverse of a Matrix and its Applications (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for every numerical problem: state the determinant, the adjoint (or row operations), the inverse, and verify your answer where asked. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define the adjoint of a square matrix and write the adjoint of A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]].
questions.answer: The adjoint of a square matrix A is the transpose of its matrix of cofactors, adj(A) = [C_ij]^T. For a 2x2 matrix A = [[a, b], [c, d]] the shortcut is adj(A) = [[d, -b], [-c, a]]: swap the diagonal entries and negate the off-diagonal entries. Hence for A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]], adj(A) = [[4, -1], [-2, 3]].

questions.question: Find the inverse of A = [[4, 3], [3, 2]].
Determine whether A = [[2, 4], [3, 6]] is singular or non-singular, and state whether it has an inverse.
questions.answer: |A| = 2x6 - 4x3 = 12 - 12 = 0. Since |A| = 0, A is a SINGULAR matrix and therefore has NO inverse. (The second row is 1.5 times the first, so the rows are dependent.)

questions.question: If A = [[a, b], [c, d]] with |A| != 0, then A^(-1) equals:
Solve the system 2x + y = 5, 3x + 2y = 8 by the matrix method.
questions.explanation: Form A X = B, invert, multiply.

questions.question: For invertible matrices A and B, (AB)^(-1) = A^(-1) B^(-1).
questions.explanation: The correct reversal law is (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1).

questions.question: Find the inverse of A = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 5, 3], [1, 0, 8]] using the adjoint method, and state the value of |A^(-1)|.

Solve the system x + y + z = 6, y + 3z = 11, x + z = 2 (equivalently x + 0y + z = 2) by the matrix method: x - 2y + z = -3 is replaced so use x + y + z = 6, x - y + z = 2, 2x + y - z = 1. Show all steps.
Using elementary row operations, outline how to find A^(-1) and give the inverse of A = [[1, 2], [1, 3]].
questions.answer: Form [A | I] = [1, 2 | 1, 0 ; 1, 3 | 0, 1] and reduce the left block to I by row operations; the right block becomes A^(-1). R2 -> R2 - R1 gives [1, 2 | 1, 0 ; 0, 1 | -1, 1]. R1 -> R1 - 2 R2 gives [1, 0 | 3, -2 ; 0, 1 | -1, 1]. Hence A^(-1) = [[3, -2], [-1, 1]]. (Check: |A| = 3 - 2 = 1, adj(A) = [[3, -2], [-1, 1]], same result.)

questions.answer: The inverse is A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|, where adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. It exists only when the matrix is square and non-singular, i.e. |A| != 0.

questions.answer: |A| = 1x4 - 2x2 = 4 - 4 = 0. Since the determinant is zero, A is singular and A^(-1) = adj(A)/|A| would require division by zero, so no inverse exists. (Row 2 is twice Row 1.)

questions.question: Find the value of x for which A = [[x, 3], [2, x]] is singular.
questions.answer: A is singular when |A| = 0. |A| = x^2 - 6 = 0, so x^2 = 6 and x = +sqrt(6) or x = -sqrt(6).

questions.question: State the property linking |A| and |A^(-1)| and use it when |A| = 5.
questions.answer: The property is |A^(-1)| = 1/|A|, which follows from |A| |A^(-1)| = |A A^(-1)| = |I| = 1. If |A| = 5, then |A^(-1)| = 1/5.

questions.question: Prove the reversal law (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1) for invertible A and B.
questions.answer: Consider the product (AB)(B^(-1) A^(-1)) = A (B B^(-1)) A^(-1) = A I A^(-1) = A A^(-1) = I. Similarly (B^(-1) A^(-1))(AB) = I. Since B^(-1) A^(-1) multiplied by AB (on both sides) gives I, by uniqueness of the inverse (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1).

questions.question: If A is invertible, show that (A^(-1))^(-1) = A.
questions.answer: By definition A^(-1) is the matrix with A A^(-1) = A^(-1) A = I. Reading this the other way, A is a matrix whose product with A^(-1) (on both sides) is I, so A satisfies the definition of the inverse of A^(-1). Since the inverse is unique, (A^(-1))^(-1) = A.

questions.question: If A is a 3x3 matrix with |A| = 2, find |adj A| and |A^(-1)|.
questions.answer: For an n x n matrix, |adj A| = |A|^(n-1). With n = 3, |adj A| = |A|^2 = 2^2 = 4. Also |A^(-1)| = 1/|A| = 1/2.

questions.question: Explain why the inverse of a matrix, when it exists, is unique.
questions.answer: Suppose B and C are both inverses of A, so AB = BA = I and AC = CA = I. Then B = B I = B (A C) = (B A) C = I C = C. Hence B = C, so the inverse is unique.

questions.question: Find the cofactor matrix of A = [[1, 0, 2], [0, 1, 0], [2, 0, 1]] and hence its adjoint.
Find the inverse of A = [[2, 3, 1], [1, 2, 3], [3, 1, 2]] using the adjoint method and verify one entry of A A^(-1).
Solve the system 2x - 3y + 5z = 11, 3x + 2y - 4z = -5, x + y - 2z = -3 by the matrix method.
Explain, with the derivation, why the solution of A X = B is X = A^(-1) B, and state what happens when A is singular.
questions.answer:
Write the linear system in matrix form as A X = B, where A is the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and B the column of constants. Suppose A is non-singular, so |A| != 0 and A^(-1) exists. Multiply BOTH sides of A X = B on the LEFT by A^(-1):
   A^(-1)(A X) = A^(-1) B.
By associativity, (A^(-1) A) X = A^(-1) B. Since A^(-1) A = I and I X = X, this gives
   X = A^(-1) B.
We must multiply on the same (left) side of both sides because matrix multiplication is not commutative. This X is the unique solution.
If A is SINGULAR (|A| = 0), then A^(-1) does not exist and this method fails. The system is then either inconsistent (no solution) or has infinitely many solutions. Which case occurs is decided by (adj A) B: if (adj A) B != O the system is inconsistent; if (adj A) B = O it has infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: Find the inverse of A = [[1, 2], [3, 7]] by elementary row operations, showing each step, and confirm the result by the adjoint method.
State and prove the property (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T for an invertible matrix A, and illustrate with A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]].
questions.answer:
Property: for an invertible matrix A, the inverse of the transpose equals the transpose of the inverse, (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T.
Proof: start from A A^(-1) = I. Take the transpose of both sides. Using (XY)^T = Y^T X^T and I^T = I:
   (A A^(-1))^T = I^T  =>  (A^(-1))^T A^T = I.
Similarly A^(-1) A = I gives A^T (A^(-1))^T = I. Hence (A^(-1))^T is a matrix which, multiplied by A^T on both sides, gives I, so by uniqueness (A^T)^(-1) = (A^(-1))^T.
Illustration: A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]], |A| = 6 - 5 = 1, A^(-1) = [[3, -1], [-5, 2]], so (A^(-1))^T = [[3, -5], [-1, 2]]. Also A^T = [[2, 5], [1, 3]], |A^T| = 1, (A^T)^(-1) = [[3, -5], [-1, 2]]. The two results match.

(iii) For k = 5, is A invertible? Give |A|.

questions.answer: (i) |A| = 6k - 6. (ii) A is singular when 6k - 6 = 0, i.e. k = 1. (iii) For k = 5, |A| = 30 - 6 = 24 != 0, so A is invertible. (iv) A singular matrix has NO inverse, because A^(-1) = adj(A)/|A| would divide by zero.

questions.question:
Passage: To find the inverse of A = [[1, 2], [2, 5]] by elementary row operations, a student forms [A | I] = [1, 2 | 1, 0 ; 2, 5 | 0, 1].
(i) What operation clears the entry below the first pivot?
(ii) Perform it and write the new second row.
(iii) What operation clears the entry above the second pivot?
(iv) Write A^(-1).
questions.answer: (i) R2 -> R2 - 2R1 clears the entry below the first pivot. (ii) New R2 = [0, 1 | -2, 1]. (iii) R1 -> R1 - 2R2 clears the entry above the second pivot, giving R1 = [1, 0 | 5, -2]. (iv) A^(-1) = [[5, -2], [-2, 1]]. (Check: |A| = 5 - 4 = 1.)

questions.answer: (i) |A| = 1x4 - 2x2 = 0. (ii) Since |A| = 0, A is singular. (iii) adj(A) = [[4, -2], [-2, 1]]; (adj A) B = [[4x3 - 2x6], [-2x3 + 1x6]] = [[0], [0]] = O. (iv) Because |A| = 0 and (adj A) B = O, the system is consistent with INFINITELY MANY solutions (the two equations are proportional).

questions.question:
Passage: A rotation matrix R = [[0, -1], [1, 0]] rotates points by 90 degrees. Rotations can be undone by inverse rotations.
(i) Find |R|.
(ii) Write adj(R).
(iii) Find R^(-1).
(iv) What geometric operation does R^(-1) represent?
questions.answer: (i) |R| = 0x0 - (-1)(1) = 1. (ii) adj(R) = [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]. (iii) R^(-1) = (1/1)[[0, 1], [-1, 0]] = [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]. (iv) R^(-1) rotates points by -90 degrees (a 90-degree rotation in the opposite direction), undoing R.
